It finds the beat on its own now.

DFP TC Burn 2.6

The warning tag is now yours to place

2.5 added a tag under the timecode when a file's timecode jumps. It sat where the app put it. From this release it is a style element in its own right, listed as Warning Tag, so it can be dragged, aligned, recoloured and resized like anything else.

  • It starts out following the timecode, exactly where it has always been drawn — so every style you already have renders unchanged. Nothing moves until you move it.
  • Drag it and it keeps the position it was already in, then stays where you put it. The geometry fields read as greyed while it is following, so you can see what will be drawn before you take it over.
  • Colour can be changed without giving up the automatic placement, and Reset puts it back on auto.
  • It is called Warning Tag, not Jump Tag, because the slot is general: a timecode jump is the only thing that raises one today, and anything added later will appear in the same place.

A tick box for whether it is burned in at all

The Output card has “Burn warning tag into picture”, ticked by default. Clear it and that render goes out without a tag.

  • It affects the picture only. The alert in the window and the watch-folder log still report the jump, so clearing it cannot hide a jump from you — only from whoever receives the file, which is now your call rather than the app's.
  • It is per render rather than saved into the style, so the next file starts with the tag on again.
  • The thumbnail follows it, so what you see is what gets written.

A bars | beats readout that finds the tempo by itself

Tick one box and the app listens to the music, works out the tempo and the downbeat, and burns a bars and beats counter into the picture — 017|3, meaning bar 17 beat 3. Nothing to type, no musical knowledge needed.

  • It analyses the program audio on a split-track file — music on one channel, timecode on the other — and takes well under a second.
  • It tells you how sure it is beside the tempo — a percentage when the answer is clean, and what is wrong with it when it is not. That is part of the answer rather than a footnote: detection is good, not infallible, and a number shown without it would invite more trust than it has earned.
  • If it is unsure it says so and still shows the count, because a tentative grid you can check beats no grid at all. If it finds nothing convincing it says that, instead of inventing a tempo.
  • It counts on the audio clock, not the timecode, so a timecode jump in the file does not disturb the beats — the music carried on, and so does the count.
  • Where the tempo moves across a track it works out how far the count will have slipped by the end, in frames, and tells you to check the last chorus. A beat played with feel in the middle costs nothing; the numbers being wrong when the track finishes is the thing worth knowing about.
  • Set the time signature yourself for music in three or six, and bar one is worked out again for the meter you chose.
  • It is a style element, Bars | Beats, so it can be placed, recoloured and sized like anything else — or switched off in a style that should never carry one.

And when it gets the beat wrong, one click fixes it

Detection is a proposal, not a verdict. Every commercial tool that does this gets it wrong sometimes and none of them pretend otherwise — what they offer is being one click from right. So does this.

  • ×2 and ÷2 for a count running at half or double the speed you want. The app will not make that call for itself: a pattern that leaves some beats empty looks exactly like counting at double speed, and only you can hear which it is.
  • The detected tempo sits in a field you can simply type over, keeping the downbeat the app found.
  • Nudge bar 1 moves the “1” onto another beat of the same bar. That is the common failure by a long way — where the tempo is right and the bar line is not — and it is one press rather than a switch to typing timecodes.
  • Corrections belong to the file they were made on. Load another and they are cleared, so one track's fix is never silently applied to the next.

4K output

540p, 720p, 1080p and now 4K (3840×2160). 540p is still the default, because it is still the review size.

  • One style renders identically at all four sizes — element sizes have always been a share of the frame rather than fixed pixels, which is why 4K needed no layout work.
  • It costs about seven times a 540p render rather than the sixteen the pixel count suggests, because only the timecode is redrawn per frame.
  • Picking 4K with ProRes now says what the file size will be, since 4K 4444 runs near 11 GB a minute. It is still allowed — just not a surprise.

One copy at a time

Launch the app when it is already open and the copy already running comes to the front, instead of a second one starting.

  • Two copies share one set of styles, assets and working draft on disk, so the second to save would quietly overwrite the first one's edits.
  • Two copies watching the same folder would both render the same dropped file to the same path, which is the failure that actually costs you something.
  • If the copy already open is a different build, the app says so before bringing it forward rather than handing you back a version you were not expecting.

It tells you when the timecode jumps.

DFP TC Burn 2.5

Timecode breaks are flagged, with the times

If the timecode in a file jumps — two takes spliced together, a recorder restarted, a re-slate — the app now says so as soon as it reads the file, and tells you where. Until now the only way to catch it was to happen to be watching the right second of the finished burn-in.

  • Each break is listed with how far into the file it is, the timecode either side of it, and how big the jump was. The time on the left is where to scrub to.
  • It advises; it never blocks. A jump is often known and intended, and the render stays available either way.
  • The burn-in itself carries a small amber line under the timecode — "(TC JUMP @ 04:50:31:13)" — so the warning travels with the video to whoever reviews it, not just with the app. Files with no jump render exactly as before.
  • Watch folders flag it too: the row is tinted, the timecodes are listed in their own line, a count appears beside Rendered/Failed/Skipped, and it goes into the folder's log. That matters more there, because nobody is watching.

It only speaks up when it means something

The decoder misses the odd frame on almost every file, and a warning that fires on those would be noise you learn to ignore.

  • A break is only reported when the timecode moved further than the audio between two frames can account for. A frame the decoder simply missed is not a break.
  • A splice is rarely frame-aligned, so the frame straddling it decodes to nonsense. Breaks that close together are reported as the one edit they actually are, not as two.

TC Burn updates itself.

DFP TC Burn 2.3

The app checks for its own updates

Until now a new build meant being sent a disk image, which meant the version actually in use was whichever one you last got round to installing. TC Burn now asks a small file on the internet whether there is a newer build — on launch, at most once a day — and offers to install it for you.

  • Help → Check for Updates… does the same thing whenever you want it.
  • The update window shows exactly these release notes before you decide.
  • You can turn the automatic half off the first time it asks.

What that costs, and what it does not

One request for a public file, and nothing else. No account, no telemetry, no report of what you render — the same promise the rest of the app makes.

  • The request says nothing about your Mac, you, or your audio.
  • An update is only installed if it carries a signature made with DF Productions' key AND is notarized by Apple under the same identity as the copy you are running. Either check failing means it is refused, not warned about.
